headline: Boots launches SureLeaf, first UK high-street medical cannabis service
dek: Boots Online Doctor opened a private, consultant-led medical cannabis service on 16 November for adults 25 and over with chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia.
key_points: UK pharmacy chain Boots launched SureLeaf on 16 November, a private online service that can prescribe cannabis-based medicines through Boots Online Doctor.
Patients must be 25 or older, have a listed chronic pain condition, generalised anxiety disorder or insomnia, and have already tried conventional treatments without enough relief.
A one-month trial costs £89 and a yearly plan £99, with the medicine itself and extra appointments charged separately, according to trade press.
The launch puts a household brand into a private market that the Care Quality Commission says more than doubled to 833,525 prescribed items in 2024-25, while major evidence reviews remain cautious.
body: Medical cannabis in the UK has just moved from specialist clinics to the high street. Boots announced on 16 November that its online pharmacy arm, Boots Online Doctor, has launched SureLeaf, a private service that assesses adults for cannabis-based medicines and, where a consultant agrees, prescribes and monitors them. The Guardian described it as a first for a British high-street pharmacy.

The service is narrow by design. It is open to people aged 25 and over with one of a list of chronic pain conditions, generalised anxiety disorder or insomnia disorder, and only after conventional treatment has failed to give adequate relief. For an industry that has spent eight years arguing that legal access exists on paper but not in practice, a chain with Boots' reach is a different kind of signal.
## What Boots is offering

According to Boots' announcement, patients start with an online assessment. A clinical team reviews whether they are suitable, and those who pass move to a video consultation with a consultant in the relevant specialty who is on the General Medical Council's Specialist Register. That requirement matters: under the 2018 change in UK law, cannabis-based medicines can only be prescribed by, or under the direction of, a specialist-register doctor.

Any proposed prescription is then checked by a multidisciplinary team that includes a second, independent consultant before treatment starts. Once a patient begins, Boots says there is a first review after 28 days and further reviews at least every three months, using validated questionnaires on quality of life, pain, anxiety, sleep and mood.

The list of eligible pain conditions is long. It runs from chronic primary and neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia to complex regional pain syndrome, back and neck pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sciatica, trigeminal neuralgia, phantom limb pain, chronic migraine, endometriosis-related pelvic pain and chronic abdominal or pancreatic pain.

Pharmacy Magazine reported that patients must have tried at least two conventional treatments, such as prescription drugs or psychotherapy, and that an online questionnaire screens out those who have not. A Boots spokesperson told The Pharmaceutical Journal that independent prescribers, including trained pharmacists, will also be part of the service.
## The price and the model

Boots is selling SureLeaf as a subscription. The Pharmacist and Pharmacy Magazine both reported a one-month trial at £89, covering an initial assessment, a 10ml starter dose and a check-in at the end of the month, and a yearly plan at £99 that covers the initial assessment and four follow-up appointments. Treatment and any extra appointments are priced separately, Pharmacy Magazine said.

That structure looks like the one most UK private clinics already use: a membership fee for the clinical side and a separate bill for the medicine. What Boots adds is distribution and trust. Mike Barnes, a consultant neurologist and founder of the Medical Cannabis Clinicians Society, told The Pharmaceutical Journal that prescribing has so far been confined largely to about 40 private clinics, and that having a company the size of Boots involved 'gives it credibility.'

Boots medical director Dr David Gwynne framed the launch carefully. 'Medical cannabis is not appropriate for everyone,' he said in the company's release, stressing safeguards and specialist oversight at every stage.
> Boots is not creating demand for medical cannabis in the UK. It is putting a familiar name on a private market that was already doubling without it.
## A market already growing fast

The numbers behind the launch come from the Care Quality Commission's annual report on controlled drugs, cited by The Pharmaceutical Journal. Private prescribing of cannabis-based products reached 833,525 items between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025, against 356,335 the year before. By MetaFlora's count that is a rise of about 134% in a single year.

The same report found that in 2024 pharmacists prescribed 441,409 cannabis-based items and doctors 209,644, which shows how much of the work is already done by independent prescribers working alongside specialists. On the NHS, by contrast, just 70 items of cannabidiol were prescribed in 2025.

That gap, a fast-growing private market and an almost absent NHS one, is the space SureLeaf is built for. Suppliers are already moving into it. Canadian producer Rubicon Organics said on 16 November that it had launched its 1964 Supply Co full-spectrum vapes in the UK medical market, part of an international business that made up 11.7% of its third-quarter revenue.
## The evidence question

Boots is entering a field where the science is still contested, and its own framing reflects that. The Pharmaceutical Journal noted that a Cochrane review published in January 2026 found no clear evidence that cannabis-based medicines work for chronic pain, and that a meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry in March 2026 found no significant effect in anxiety. The charity Pain Concern told the journal there is not yet enough evidence to support these drugs in chronic pain management and called for more research.

Boots' answer is data. Alongside the launch, it is exploring a research programme with the University of Nottingham that would look at patient outcomes, prescribing practices and experience in chronic pain. The university confirmed the plan on its own news page. Because every SureLeaf patient fills in structured questionnaires at set intervals, the service could produce one of the larger real-world datasets in UK cannabis medicine, if the programme goes ahead and the results are published.

Regulators have also been looking at pharmacy practice. In October 2025 the General Pharmaceutical Council reviewed 25 pharmacies that regularly supply cannabis-based products and found most were meeting standards, but called for better information sharing between clinics, suppliers and pharmacies, The Pharmaceutical Journal reported.
## How it compares with Germany

The UK and Germany are Europe's two largest medical cannabis markets, and they are moving in different directions. Germany removed cannabis flower from statutory health insurance cover on 30 July 2026, and a pending bill, Bundestag printed paper 21/3061, would require an in-person consultation before flower can be prescribed and would end mail-order delivery of flower. The UK, which has never covered cannabis on the NHS in any volume, is instead seeing large retail brands move into private telemedicine.
For producers that sell into both, the UK's private, consultant-gated model is becoming the steadier channel while Germany's rules are rewritten.
## What to watch

First, uptake: Boots has not said how many patients it expects, and the CQC's next controlled-drugs report will show whether private prescribing keeps rising. Second, the University of Nottingham programme: whether it is formally agreed and what it measures. Third, competition: whether other pharmacy chains or online doctors follow with similar services. And fourth, the evidence base, which professional bodies will keep weighing against fast commercial growth. Industry and clinicians meet again at the Cannabis Health Symposium in London on 26 November.
